record.title: PUN reports noise-aware planning results on geometric 2D–4D benchmarks
record.summary: A new preprint introduces Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that maps obstacle geometry, goal, cost and noise inputs to a desirability field, then uses bounded local search to guide stochastic replanning. On the authors’ 4D geometric benchmark it reports 95–100% success at 10.51–11.66 ms/start across four tested noise levels. The paper says compared methods share the saved test queries and noise sequence, but PUN timings use a B200 GPU while listed baseline timings use faster CPU implementations; only one trained model per dimension is evaluated. The method assumes control–noise matching, and the authors report no full robot/contact models and continued difficulty on adversarial mazes. These are credible but unconfirmed paper-reported results, not a demonstrated robotics deployment.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), which learns a geometry-conditioned desirability/value field from partially converged Walk-on-Stars Monte Carlo labels and uses bounded local search over the learned field for replanning under control execution noise. The derivation relies on a control–noise matching assumption.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s 4D replanning benchmark, PUN reports success rates of 100%, 100%, 100% and 95% across noise levels λ=0.25, 1, 2 and 4, with reported runtime 10.63, 10.51, 10.55 and 11.66 ms/start. At λ=4 the listed A* baseline reports 59.17% success and 62.44 ms/start; other baselines also have lower reported success and longer listed runtimes. These are paper-reported geometric simulation results, with PUN GPU timings and CPU baseline timings.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Appendix D.1 says replanning methods share saved environment-goal queries and Gaussian noise sequences; the 4D set uses 480 maps with three goals and one start per goal. The authors report one trained model per dimension and map-level bootstrap intervals; repeated model-training seeds are not reported.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper states its experiments do not include full robot models with contact, are restricted to settings where control and noise are matched, and find adversarial maze-like geometries challenging. Its reflecting-boundary value field is also evaluated in collision-failure rollouts, which the authors say is not the exact value function for that execution model.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: No independent reproduction, verified code artifact, physical-robot evaluation, contact-rich manipulation result, or transfer beyond the paper’s control–noise-matched geometric benchmarks is established by this review.

evidence_gaps.description: The 4D benchmark, reported success rates and runtime results have not been independently reproduced, and only one trained model per dimension is reported.
The paper’s key control–noise matching assumption and collision-failure execution evaluation limit transfer to realistic robot dynamics.
Published runtime comparisons use a B200 GPU for PUN and CPU implementations for the baseline methods.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported gains hold beyond the studied geometry benchmarks and control–noise-matched regime, a learned value field with local search could reduce the cost of stochastic planning in higher-dimensional workspaces without solving a PDE for each instance. This is a potentially useful robotics-research result, while physical deployment, contact-rich robots and transfer outside the matching assumption remain unestablished.
limitations: The screened-Poisson derivation requires a control–noise matching assumption, and experiments are restricted to settings where the authors consider that assumption reasonable.
No full robot models with contact or physical robot trials are included; transfer to contact-rich manipulation is untested.
The authors state adversarial geometries such as mazes remain challenging because long corridors can produce weak or poorly resolved learned gradients.

The field is derived for reflecting boundaries, while experiments count obstacle collisions as rollout failures; the authors note this is not the exact value function for the collision-failure execution model.
Appendix D.1 reports one trained model per dimension; bootstrap resampling of maps quantifies query-set uncertainty but does not establish training-seed variability or independent replication.
Table 5 compares PUN GPU timings with CPU timings for the listed baselines; hardware and implementation differ, so the runtime ratios are not hardware-normalized.
No official artifact or independent reproduction surfaced in this activation’s bounded search; absence from search results is not proof that none exists.
brief.summary: A new preprint introduces Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that maps obstacle geometry, goal, cost and noise inputs to a desirability field, then uses bounded local search to guide stochastic replanning. On the authors’ 4D geometric benchmark it reports 95–100% success at 10.51–11.66 ms/start across four tested noise levels. The paper says compared methods share the saved test queries and noise sequence, but PUN timings use a B200 GPU while listed baseline timings use faster CPU implementations; only one trained model per dimension is evaluated. The method assumes control–noise matching, and the authors report no full robot/contact models and continued difficulty on adversarial mazes. These are credible but unconfirmed paper-reported results, not a demonstrated robotics deployment.

technical.claimed_result: The 4D replanning table reports 95–100% success and 10.51–11.66 ms/start across λ=0.25, 1, 2, 4. At λ=4 the authors report 95% for PUN versus 59.17% for A*, 59.17% for Dijkstra, 85.83% for RRT, 71.67% for MPPI and 78.33% for PI²-CMA. Listed runtimes are 11.66 ms/start for PUN versus 62.44, 59.39, 38.31, 374.83 and 356.72 ms/start, respectively.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary preprint establishes that the authors published this method, protocol and reported benchmark values. the research desk has not independently verified the numerical results or run the method.
technical.mechanism: PUN derives a screened-Poisson desirability problem under linearly solvable stochastic optimal control, uses reflecting Neumann conditions at obstacles and a goal Dirichlet boundary, extends Walk-on-Stars supervision to higher dimensions, trains a Fourier neural operator from noisy partially converged labels, and performs bounded grid-local search over the predicted field before executing a short prefix and replanning.
technical.novelty: Combines reflecting-boundary Walk-on-Stars labels, neural-operator amortization across geometries and bounded local search to guide stochastic replanning; the paper’s most consequential evidence here is its author-reported 4D benchmark, not a physical deployment.
technical.regime: Synthetic/geometric 2D–4D stochastic path-planning benchmarks. The 4D replanning test has 480 maps, three goals per map and one start per goal; all compared methods use the same saved queries/noise sequence. The paper reports one trained model per dimension. Dynamics assume isotropic noise matched to control cost (Σ=λI in the specialized regime); rollouts count collisions and outer-boundary violations as failures.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint gives detailed benchmark and timing protocols, reports paired-map bootstrap intervals and matched query/noise samples, but evaluates one trained model per dimension. A targeted exact-title/arXiv-ID search and inspection of the paper surfaced no official code artifact or independent reproduction. the research desk did not run the code or reproduce results.
technical.strongest_baseline: At λ=4 in 4D, RRT has the closest reported success rate among the listed methods (85.83% versus PUN 95%) and uses 38.31 ms/start versus PUN 11.66 ms/start. All listed comparator runtimes in this table use CPU implementations because they were faster than their GPU counterparts; PUN uses GPU timing, so the runtime comparison is implementation-and-device specific. A* is an important counterpoint at lower noise and reports 100% success at λ=0.25 and 96.67% at λ=1.

brief.title: PUN reports noise-aware planning results on geometric 2D–4D benchmarks
brief.why_it_matters: A learned global value field paired with bounded test-time search could make stochastic planning over unseen higher-dimensional geometries less dependent on a per-instance PDE solve. The reported benchmark is promising and directly relevant to robotics planning research, but its transfer depends on a restrictive control–noise matching regime and has not been tested on contact-rich physical robots. Cross-device runtimes should not be read as a hardware-normalized speed comparison.
